 NPS Swasthya: How the new healthcare savings model works
 Aprajita Sharma 6 min read 5 Oct 2026, 03:54 PM IST 
 Summary
 NPS Swasthya combines a healthcare investment account with a mandatory super top-up health insurance policy. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A medical emergency can derail financial planning, particularly during retirement, when income may be limited, and healthcare costs can rise sharply. Keeping that in mind, the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) launched NPS Swasthya on 1 October, NPS Diwas.
 It combines a healthcare investment account with a mandatory super top-up health insurance policy.
 The proposition is different from simply buying a health insurance policy. Under NPS Swasthya, the subscriber builds a corpus that can be used to meet healthcare expenses, including the deductible under the super top-up policy. This means the subscriber does not have to arrange the deductible entirely from other savings when a claim arises.
 Subscribers can also transfer funds from their existing National Pension System (NPS) account under the All Citizen Model to the Swasthya account.
 To enrol, an individual must first open an NPS Swasthya Investment Account. The subscriber has to deposit ₹ 1,000 towards investment, pay an annual Health Benefit Administrator (HBA) maintenance charge of ₹ 200 and the first-year health insurance premium. The PFRDA has appointed Medi Assist as the first HBA.
 Thereafter, the minimum contribution is ₹ 10 per annum. The renewal premium can also be funded from the NPS Swasthya corpus, subject to the subscriber’s mandate.
 How the insurance component works
 Any individual eligible to join NPS can enrol in NPS Swasthya. The health insurance component is offered as a group policy, with the PFRDA as the master policyholder.
 Subscribers can take coverage for themselves or extend it to up to two adults and two dependent children. The entry age for the insurance is 18 to 70 years, while renewal is permitted up to and including 85 years.
 The policy is a super top-up, which means the insurer starts paying only after the specified deductible is met. The deductible varies with the sum insured: ₹ 10,000 for a ₹ 1 lakh sum insured, ₹ 50,000 for a ₹ 5 lakh sum insured, ₹ 1 lakh for a ₹ 10 lakh sum insured, and ₹ 3 lakh for a ₹ 30 lakh sum insured.
 Premiums are divided into three age cohorts: 18-40 years, 41-60 years and 61-70 years.
 For instance, a ₹ 30 lakh sum insured with a ₹ 3 lakh deductible costs ₹ 1,732 for those aged 18-40 years, ₹ 2,523 for those aged 41-60 years and ₹ 4,953 for those aged 61-70 years, according to PFRDA data. Currently, Aditya Birla Health Insurance offers it through the Axis Pension Fund.
 “Premiums are 30-40% cheaper than competing plans available in the market,” said PFRDA chairperson S. Ramann.
 However, a direct comparison with retail super top-up policies is difficult because a similar combination of sum insured and deductible is not readily available in the market. Some products offer a closer comparison.
 At ICICI Lombard, a ₹ 25 lakh sum insured with a ₹ 3 lakh deductible costs ₹ 5,125 for a 40-year-old, ₹ 13,377 for a 60-year-old and ₹ 24,398 for a 70-year-old.
 “Deductible amount matters more in super top-up than sum insured. The higher the deductible, the lower the premium. Comparing premiums with the industry, NPS super top-up premiums are quite reasonable,” said Akshay Bansal, a certified financial planner and founder of Money Plant Project, a financial advisory firm.
 The premium, however, is only one part of the comparison. A key differentiator is the entry age. Not all insurers offer super top-up policies with entry permitted up to 70 years. This relatively high entry age could help individuals who find it difficult to obtain health insurance at older ages.
 Also, since it is a group policy, there is no requirement for medical tests at the time of enrolment. However, subscribers have to make the correct declaration of pre-existing diseases for all covered members. “PEDs will have a waiting period of one year,” said Ramann.
 That does not mean everyone will necessarily be able to buy the cover. “Around 15 diseases, such as cancer and heart attack, have been identified, which will either be excluded or get coverage on paying an extra premium, subject to insurers' underwriting guidelines,” said Ramann.
 Premium comparison with other health products is important as well. Viresh Patel, a Mumbai-based Sebi-registered investment adviser, said he would compare premiums for fixed-benefit and investment-linked health products offered by life insurers before recommending one to his clients. Although the products are not directly comparable, their pros and cons should be assessed individually to determine suitability.
 “I will compare premiums of Swasthya with policies such as LIC Jeevan Aarogya and ICICI Pru Hospital Care that offer a fixed sum on hospitalization, or ICICI Pru Health Saver that combines hospitalization cover with a market-linked savings fund,” he said. Although the products are not directly comparable, their pros and cons should be assessed at an individual level to determine suitability.
 Role of the investment account
 The Swasthya investment account is meant to help subscribers build a healthcare corpus. This corpus can be used to meet the deductible when the super top-up is triggered, or to cover eligible outpatient department (OPD) expenses, provided the service is within the HBA network.
 However, the biggest drawback is that subscribers can only make partial withdrawals of up to 25% of their contributions. There is no restriction on the number of withdrawals and no minimum waiting period between withdrawals. Payments will be settled directly with the hospital or other eligible healthcare service providers.

docs.title: IDCW vs SWP: which of these options should retirees choose and why
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 IDCW vs SWP: which of these options should retirees choose and why
 Rounaq Neroy 5 min read 5 Oct 2026, 01:23 PM IST 
 Summary
 IDCW payouts from mutual funds are neither guaranteed nor necessarily tax-efficient. For retirees seeking regular cash flows, a disciplined SWP can offer greater control over withdrawals and taxation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Recently, at dinner, I met individuals in their 50s, nearing retirement, and those who had already hung up their work boots. The hot topic was the rising cost of living and how to meet cash-flow needs during the golden years.
 While most had built a sizeable corpus by investing in equity mutual funds over the years, some, particularly those in their 60s, had chosen the ‘Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal’ or IDCW option (erstwhile referred to as the dividend option), hoping to earn regular income to meet retirement expenses.
 I was surprised by this and explained why this may not be a definitive way to address cash-flow needs.
 IDCW myths
 The fact is, IDCW payouts are not guaranteed, unlike interest-earning fixed-income instruments, and are often at the discretion of the mutual fund house and fund manager .
 As per Sebi regulations, the scheme needs to generate a distributable surplus to declare an IDCW payout. Even if there is a distributable surplus, it does not obligate the fund manager to declare and give the payout.
 In challenging years, if the scheme has not fared well, the fund may not announce an IDCW payout. Even if you have invested in a scheme under the “monthly IDCW” option, it only indicates the frequency at which the fund house reviews the scheme for potential distribution; it does not guarantee regular monthly payouts.
 So, the IDCW option is not a sure-shot way of expecting regular and predictable cash flows during retirement.
 It is also incorrect to assume that, like dividend yield in stocks, IDCW payouts in mutual funds work the same way. That is completely untrue. The IDCW payout comes from accumulated profits or the investors’ investment value, unlike stocks, where the company distributes profits by way of dividends to shareholders.
 After the abolition of the Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT), IDCW payouts are taxed as ‘income from other sources’ as per your income-tax slab.
 If the IDCW payout from a single mutual fund house exceeds ₹ 10,000 in a financial year, initially, tax deduction at source (TDS) at 10% will take place, which will be adjusted when you file your Income-tax Return (ITR). If the PAN is not provided, the TDS rate doubles to 20%. The TDS rate is applied to the entire payout amount, not just the portion exceeding ₹ 10,000.
 If you are in a higher income-tax slab, this can make IDCW a deterrent and a tax-inefficient option.
 A better route
 So, what is a better option for retirees or those looking for cash flows?
 Choosing the growth option, where the fund manager reinvests profits back into the scheme, remains suitable for compounding wealth, along with opting for a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP). This facility allows you to withdraw money from a scheme systematically, monthly, quarterly, biannually, etc.
 All you have to do is choose the frequency based on your cash-flow needs and set a prudent withdrawal rate. This gives you predictable cash flows and better control, unlike the variable and non-guaranteed IDCW option.
 How much should the SWP rate be? Around 3-4% is ideal. In the initial years, the SWP rate may be 3%, depending on the corpus, and later, if the scheme is clocking a decent annualised growth rate, the rate may be increased to 4%.
 This needs to be done carefully; otherwise, the corpus may not be enough for the remaining years of life. Arbitrarily increasing the SWP rate raises the risk of exhausting the corpus sooner, particularly during prolonged downturns.
 It is important that the schemes from which you are making systematic withdrawals are performing well, ideally clocking a much higher rate than the withdrawal rate.
 It is best to remain conservative. A 3% withdrawal rate is the thumb rule that helps ensure you do not run out of money, or exhaust the mutual fund corpus, during retirement .
 You also need to account for inflation, since it erodes the purchasing power of hard-earned money, estimate your monthly retirement expenses, determine the retirement corpus needed at the given withdrawal rate and then go ahead with the SWP.
 For example, your present monthly expenses at age 56 are ₹ 55,000, inflation is 6% per annum on average, and you have four years before you hang up your work boots. In this case, your monthly retirement expenses will likely increase to about ₹ 69,436, or around ₹ 8.3 lakh annually.
 Given this, your retirement corpus should at least be around ₹ 2.78 crore.
 Now, say you have built this corpus by wisely investing in equity mutual funds. It is from this amount that you need to systematically withdraw annually. At a 3% rate, the first-year withdrawal would be around ₹ 8.33 lakh annually. This would change year after year depending on how the scheme fares.
 If the NAV moves up, the corpus lasts for more years; if performance is not very good, it may last for fewer years. Hence, you also need to track how the scheme from which you are doing an SWP is performing.
 Keep in mind that if you increase the withdrawal rate beyond the thumb rule, the corpus will last far less. There is a risk of outliving the corpus and being unable to meet expenses during retirement.
 Tax-efficient withdrawals 
 Only the capital gain or profit component of systematic withdrawals is subject to capital gains tax.
 Gains on equity mutual fund investments withdrawn within 12 months of investment are treated as Short Term Capital Gains (STCG) and taxed at 20%.

Global 
 The mighty American consumer is crashing through inflation and driving growth
 Jeanne Whalen , Matt Grossman , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:47 AM IST 
 Summary
 Spending is rising because prices are climbing and Americans are buying more stuff. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 CHICAGO—Happy hour at Chicago’s Bar Roma was buzzing this past week as locals poured in for $10 cocktails and $11 bruschetta. Kathleen Harper and her husband would normally share a few appetizers, but tonight they were splurging on the $50 tasting menu.
 “After a long day—I work from home—I like to just get out of the house,” said Harper, who sells fraud-protection services. “Business has been good,” she added, “because fraud, unfortunately, is up.” She worries about the overall health of the economy and rising prices for gas and groceries, but feels secure enough to enjoy a good happy-hour deal.
 Decisions like that across the economy show America’s appetite for consumption is expanding. Americans are spending more on food, travel, couches, Halloween decor and most anything else they want or need—pushing through inflation and their own gloomy feelings about the economy.
 The dollar amount spent by U.S. households rose by 6.1% in the 12 months through August, up from annual growth of 4.3% at the end of last year, the Commerce Department reported. Economic growth for the second quarter of 2026, the most recent data available, was revised upward this past week, fueled by consumer spending and business investment.
 “For all the talk about AI data centers, the main engine of growth for GDP in the United States has been broad-based consumer spending growth, which I think is tied to a broad-based, stable labor market,” Austan Goolsbee, head of the Chicago Fed, told journalists after an economic forum this past week.
 Hiring slowed last month, though the unemployment rate remains low.
 Spending is rising because prices are climbing and Americans are buying more stuff. Just over half the spending increase in the year through August owes to the persistent inflation that has frustrated many shoppers: Consumer prices were up by about 3.4% over that period. But inflation-adjusted spending climbed by 2.6%, too, extending a streak of steady growth over the past five years.
 Supporting all that consumption is an economy that might frustrate Americans but is nonetheless keeping spending habits afloat. The job market has cooled from the postpandemic surge, but remains sturdy, with unemployment hovering at historically low rates.
 Meanwhile, many older Americans who own homes and stocks have benefited from soaring prices for both. A larger net worth might not mean a higher monthly income, but it has made many people comfortable spending a bit more than they would otherwise.
 Upbeat spending is particularly remarkable because it seems to contradict downbeat consumer sentiment. Long-running gauges of consumers’ moods are running near historic lows, weighed down by high gasoline prices, subdued hiring and contentious politics. Lousy consumer moods once correlated with lower consumer spending, but since the pandemic, sentiment has increasingly decoupled from spending and other economic indicators, economists say.
 The University of Michigan’s monthly sentiment index is just a hair above a record-low level it touched earlier this year. A similar survey, by research group The Conference Board, turned in its lowest reading in 12 years last month.
 “The macro numbers look good…spending looks good. And no one is happy,” said Brian Fabes, senior fellow at the research group NORC at the University of Chicago.
 Fabes attributed much of the spending to high earners, while Americans in the middle search for value and those at the bottom scrape to get by. For the poor, “spending isn’t actually a choice,” Fabes said. “You can’t not buy food. You can’t not buy housing.”
 Down the street from Bar Roma at a high-end furniture store, retired lawyer Alice Withaar, 65 years old, was looking for a sofa, a coffee table and two side chairs. “I’ve lived with my old stuff for a long time and it’s time for a refresh,” she said.
 Rising prices bother her. At lunch with a friend, they grumbled about everything being “twice as expensive,” Withaar said. But her old sofa is threadbare, and she no longer has to worry about pets ruining her furniture, so she is ready for an upgrade. “I don’t mean I have unlimited money,” she added. But she is able to spend “whatever it’s worth to me.”
 A survey by the New York Fed suggests spending growth has been fairly even across income groups. People who earned less than $50,000 said that their spending rose by 4.7% in the year through August, while those who made more than $100,000 said their spending grew by 4.4%.
 Charlie Zhang, 30, a charity fundraiser who was canvassing for donations near Bar Roma, said he was trying to bounce back after getting into credit-card debt and declaring bankruptcy. He earns $24 an hour, giving him just enough to split his $2,800 rent with a roommate and to cover his Taco Bell habit and an occasional Uber.
 Zhang has been trying to save by cooking more at home, or at least picking up his fast food rather than paying for delivery. “When I’m home and I’m exhausted, I’m like, ‘I can’t spend $30 for, like, a burrito right now. I got to just go walk over there.’” When he thinks about the future he feels “pretty down,” he said.
 Wealthier Americans have a rosier outlook. Since May 2025, consumer sentiment has risen for people who own the most stocks, while it has fallen for those who don’t own any, according to Joanne Hsu, director of the Michigan survey. During that stretch, the broad S&P 500 stock index has handed investors a roughly 32% return.
 Because spending is growing faster than disposable income, it might stall as people face the limits of what they have in

docs.title: Mint Explainer | Why Karnataka’s gig worker law has put platforms and workers at odds
docs.text:
Explainer 
 Mint Explainer | Why Karnataka’s gig worker law has put platforms and workers at odds
 Nabodita Ganguly 3 min read 5 Oct 2026, 01:15 PM IST 
 Summary
 At the heart of the dispute is a question: can states create their own social-security regimes for gig workers when Parliament has already enacted a national law covering them? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Karnataka’s gig worker law has emerged as a bone of contention between companies and workers. While worker unions are pushing for its implementation, companies are challenging the legislation in court. 
 At the heart of the dispute is a question with implications beyond Karnataka: can states create their own social-security regimes for gig workers when Parliament has already enacted a national law covering them? Mint explains 
 What exactly is Karnataka's gig worker law? 
 The Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025, which received the governor’s assent on 11 September 2025, creates a legal framework for ride-hailing, food delivery, logistics and other platform-based work in the state. It seeks to protect gig workers while retaining their status as independent contractors rather than classifying them as traditional employees. 
 The law, among other things, places obligations on aggregators covering social security, occupational health and safety, transparency in automated decision-making, and dispute resolution. 
 Why are new-age companies challenging it? 
 Several platforms including Uber, Swiggy , Zepto, and the Internet and Mobile Association of India (IAMAI) have moved the Karnataka High Court challenging the constitutional validity of Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers. 
 One of their main arguments is that Parliament has already enacted the Code on Social Security, 2020, (law that combines nine central labour statutes into one unified system) to create a uniform national framework governing social security for all categories of workers, including gig and platform workers. Meanwhile, the state says the Act supplements the Code. 
 A key reason for this overlap is that labour and social security fall under the Concurrent List, so both Parliament and the States may legislate. 
 “Under Article 254, a State law repugnant to a Central law on the same subject is void to the extent of repugnancy, unless it has Presidential assent,” said Malak Bhatt, Chamber Head at law firm Chambers of Malak Bhatt. “Platforms say the Code occupies the field; the State says its Act supplements it. The High Court has asked whether the two can be harmoniously construed.” 
 Why is the welfare fee contentious? 
 The platforms also challenged the welfare fee they are required to pay towards benefits for gig workers, which platforms again highlight, overlaps with the Centre’s Code on Social Security, 2020. 
 The Act originally provided for a fee of 1% to 5% of the amount paid to workers for each transaction. The government later set the rate at 1% for food and grocery delivery services. For ride-hailing platforms, the levy was fixed at 50 paise per two-wheeler trip and 75 paise per three-wheeler trip. 
 Some platforms such as Eternal , Swiggy, Zepto and Meesho have already deposited the welfare fee mandated under Karnataka’s gig-worker law. 
 What are the worker unions saying? 
 The Indian Federation of App-based Transport Workers (IFAT) and the Karnataka App-based Workers Union (KAWU) have written to the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers Welfare Board on 1 October seeking the formal implementation of the state’s gig worker law. The unions have urged the Board to convene an urgent meeting to discuss and formally adopt welfare schemes under the Act. Mint has seen a copy of the letter. 
 In its letter, the IFAT and KAWU said platforms have deposited the welfare fee with the Karnataka High Court, and urged that the money be released for gig workers. "Such amounts should be utilised in favour of the gig and platform workers as there is a dire need on the part of gig workers and no stay has been granted by the Hon'ble High Court either," it said. 
 Can the Act still be enacted with different companies challenging it? 
 Legal experts argue that the Act and Rules are in force. The Welfare Board was constituted on 27 January 2026, and a welfare fee mechanism has been notified. On 3 July 2026, the High Court declined to stay the Act, directed petitioner platforms to deposit the second quarter fee with its registry, and restrained coercive action against them subject to that deposit. 
 “A pending challenge does not by itself suspend a statute; it continues to operate unless the court orders otherwise,” said Bhatt. 
 What happens if more states make their own gig-worker laws? 
 Since labour is a Concurrent List subject, states can frame such laws; Rajasthan and Bihar have already done so. However, if more states introduce their own laws, platforms could face different rules. 
 “For platforms operating across India, however, the emergence of different State-level contribution, benefit and compliance regimes could create a patchwork of obligations,” said Ketan Mukhija, partner and co head, PE & VC, Kochhar & Co. 
 “A harmonised national framework, with room for appropriate State-specific measures, would ultimately provide greater certainty for businesses while ensuring consistent and portable social-security protection for gig workers,” Mukhija said.

Explainer Mint Explainer | Why Adani’s Mumbai airport redevelopment has triggered a row Abhishek Law 5 min read 5 Oct 2026, 11:01 AM IST Summary Adani-led MIAL proposes a 33% cut in international departures starting 25 October. Airlines reject the forced shift to Navi Mumbai Airport, citing arbitrary slot cuts, locked-in winter schedules, and lack of consultation. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now The redevelopment of Mumbai airport’s Terminal 1 has sparked a standoff between operator Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL), controlled by Adani group, and airlines over managing international flights during the transition. MIAL has proposed temporarily discontinuing 265 of 770 weekly international departure slots at Terminal 2 from 25 October, affecting 46 airlines. The slots are to be transferred to Adani-run Navi Mumbai International Airport, 50 kms away, to free up space for domestic traffic displaced from T1. With airlines rejecting the proposal and the civil aviation ministry scheduled to hold a meeting on 6 October, here is a breakdown of the conflict and its impact on passengers. What is the core dispute? Airlines say MIAL's initial communication was about transferring existing international operations from Mumbai to Navi Mumbai. The latest plan, however, proposes temporarily discontinuing 33% of international departures. An airline with 10 international departures a week from Mumbai would lose roughly three. A transfer involves moving an operation to another airport; a slot reduction means capacity at Mumbai itself is being withdrawn. MIAL says the transition to Navi Mumbai is temporary, and airlines can relocate operations at their discretion. However, the link between accommodating T1 domestic traffic and slashing 265 T2 international slots remains unclear. Where did the 33% reduction figure come from? MIAL's transition plan, previously shared with airlines and reviewed by Mint , gives airlines the option to temporarily discontinue. That is mathematically about 34.4%, although the proposal has been described as a 33% reduction. What the transition document does not spell out is the detailed capacity calculation behind the number. The Airline Operators Committee-Mumbai (AOC) has asked for the current capacity of T1 and T2, the specific constraints requiring the reduction, details of the proposed T2 enhancement and the demand-capacity analysis supporting the move. Who decides which airline slots get cut? MIAL has asked airlines to identify, by 4 pm on 6 October, the international departure slots they wish to shift or discontinue. If they do not, the airport operator has said it may select the slots based on operational and capacity considerations. These slots can be transferred to Navi Mumbai or discontinued till the new terminal at Mumbai is ready for operations. The AOC has rejected this, calling it arbitrary. Airlines say their Winter 2026-27 (from October - March next year) schedules were approved in June 2026, with fleet deployments, routes, ticket sales, and commercial commitments already locked in. The dispute is therefore also about who determines which established operations are withdrawn and on what basis that decision is made. Why do airlines claim a lack of consultation? Airlines support the redevelopment of T1 but said discussions about redevelopment should not be treated as consent to a specific reduction in international slots or a relocation. AOC claim to seek detailed discussions on the technical basis for T1 redevelopment, structural assessment, capacity impact, phasing and timelines. MIAL disputes the characterisation. Its 3 October release says “extensive consultations with airlines on the future of Terminal 1 have been ongoing since 2020” and that the redevelopment was presented to Airports Economic and Regulatory Authority of India and incorporated into the approved tariff framework. International Air Transport Association (IATA) has also called for a transition based on operational readiness, stakeholder buy-in and regulatory oversight, supporting the airlines. What changed between September 2025 and October 2026? The AOC has cited minutes of a September 2025 CSMIA Master Plan Project Phasing meeting, which indicated that T1 redevelopment was expected to follow the operationalisation of Navi Mumbai’s Terminal 2, expected around 2029. The current plan brings restrictions forward to October 2026, with T1 redevelopment scheduled to begin in January 2027. MIAL cited safety concerns for T1 which is about 60 years old. Phase one involves the north section of T1B, which represents about one-third of T1 capacity. The operator says only about 5 million of Mumbai airport’s 55 million annual passengers, or 9%, will be temporarily deoperationalised, leaving 91% unaffected. How does this impact passengers? If an airline shifts a flight from Mumbai to Navi Mumbai, passengers would need to be informed and arrangements made. A change in airport could affect connection times or require a different itinerary. There is also a cost issue. Navi Mumbai’s user development fee is higher at ₹ 1,225 for an international departing passenger, compared with ₹ 615 for that at Mumbai. Navi Mumbai plans to offer a 100% discount on landing fees for new international flights. It also plans to offer cash vouchers to international passengers to offset the difference in the fee. News 
 38 years after Ahmedabad crash, Air India seeks fast hearing on compensation formula
 Krishna Yadav 4 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The outcome could shape how compensation is determined in future air-crash cases, with victims arguing that awards should reflect actual economic loss, including income and future earning capacity, as well as inflation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Thirty-eight years after an Indian Airlines flight crashed near Ahmedabad, killing 133 people, Air India has asked the Supreme Court to fast-track a hearing in a compensation dispute whose outcome could reshape how India compensates victims of air crashes.
 The apex court is scheduled to hear the plea on Monday, according to the cause list, after Air India filed its application on 1 October. At the heart of the dispute is a simple question: should families of air-crash victims continue to be compensated using formulas developed for road-accident victims under the Motor Vehicles Act, or should courts adopt a separate framework for aviation accidents?
 The outcome could shape how compensation is determined in future air-crash cases, with victims arguing that awards should reflect actual economic loss, including income and future earning capacity, as well as inflation. They also contend that compensation should account for airlines’ financial capacity and insurance cover, rather than being restricted by formulas developed for road accidents.
 "The decision could have implications beyond compensation for plane-crash victims, as it could shape the broader framework for consumer protection and how victims are compensated for harm," said Satyam Dwivedi, aviation law specialist and managing partner at DC Law Offices.
 Air India told the Supreme Court in September 2025 to keep the underlying question of law open for consideration in connected or future proceedings.
 The compensation dispute has been pending before the top court since 2010, after litigation arising from the 19 October 1988 crash travelled from the lower court in Ahmedabad to the Gujarat High Court and eventually to the Supreme Court.
 Emails seeking comments from Air India on Sunday morning and the Airports Authority of India (AAI) remained unanswered at the time of publication.
 Different framework 
 In written submissions filed in October 2025 and reviewed by Mint, the victims argued that compensation in an air-crash case should not be calculated using the Motor Vehicles Act framework used for road accidents. They said aviation accidents are fundamentally different because passengers have no control over an aircraft's operation or safety.
 Instead, they argued that compensation should account for the victim's actual economic loss, including income, future earning capacity and changes in earnings, as well as inflation.
The victims also argued that airlines are large, financially capable and insured enterprises, and that compensation in an air crash should therefore not be restricted by formulas developed for road accidents. They said the availability of insurance should also be considered while ensuring that victims receive full and just compensation.
 The plea also pointed to the 2010 Mangalore air-crash case, in which the Supreme Court applied principles under the Motor Vehicles Act to determine compensation. The victims, however, argued that the court did not specifically decide whether the MVA framework should apply to air-crash claims, leaving the issue open.
 Case could set a precedent 
 Lawyers say the case could ultimately have implications beyond compensation payable in the 1988 crash.
 ``This is a very important case, and the Supreme Court should use this opportunity under Article 142 to lay down standardised guidelines for compensation. You cannot put a different value on a person's life based on whether they travelled by air or road,'' said Dwivedi.
 Alay Razvi, managing partner at Accord Juris, said a more individualised approach could potentially increase compensation exposure in some cases.
 “If the Supreme Court requires a more individualised assessment of actual loss, compensation exposure may increase in cases involving young victims, high-income earners, professionals with demonstrable career growth or families with substantial financial dependency. Airlines may also face greater exposure where liability is shared with other parties but is not subject to an applicable statutory or convention-based limit,” Razvi said.
 Case history 
 The case dates back to 19 October 1988, when Indian Airlines Flight IC-113, operating from Mumbai to Ahmedabad, crashed while approaching Ahmedabad airport. The aircraft was carrying 135 people, including six crew members. Of these, 133 were killed, while two passengers survived, one of whom suffered substantial physical and mental disabilities.
 Families of the deceased and survivors filed 38 civil suits between 1989 and 1992 seeking compensation. The Ahmedabad City Civil Court decided the claims in 2002. The litigation then moved to the Gujarat High Court, which decided the appeals in 2009 and revised several awards.
 The dispute reached the Supreme Court in 2010. In April that year, the court recorded that the compensation determined against Indian Airlines had been deposited with the Ahmedabad City Civil Court, along with interest, while the Airports Authority of India had deposited 30% of the compensation. The court directed disbursement to claimants subject to them furnishing security other than a bank guarantee.
 Despite the passage of nearly four decades, the dispute has remained unresolved, prompting Air India to seek an early hearing before the Supreme Court.
 The hearing comes against the backdrop of the Air India crash last year that killed 260 people, with several related pleas concerning air safety and the investigation into the crash pending before the Supreme C

Opinion 
 Must Tata Sons go public? India’s central bank has several other options that could be explored
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 5 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 It’s unclear if the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) can actually force corporate entities such as Tata Sons to list their shares for public trading. Many other ways exist for this regulator to secure the financial system’s security without heavy-handed intervention. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Regulatory pressure from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata Group of companies, to list its shares has opened up a can of worms. 
 The central bank’s directive to a company to take a particular corporate action has raised questions of regulatory jurisdiction, governance limits and the propriety of a monetary authority forcing an issue related to the equity market. 
 What makes the RBI order even more controversial is that it comes two years after Tata Sons applied for de-registration as an upper-layer non-banking finance company (NBFC); in the meantime, RBI changed the rules of the game and is now insistent that the company goes public. 
 Adding controversy to this messy situation is the fact that the central bank has not felt it necessary to clearly spell out its rationale compelling Tata Sons to pursue an initial public offering, especially since Tata Sons has paid down its outstanding debts. 
 The central bank’s diktat is being viewed in several quarters as regulatory overreach for a number of reasons. 
 First, it is unclear whether RBI can force a company to go public, especially when it is not a bank, a non-bank lender or an entity engaged in any manner of financial services as either a loan originator or distribution platform. 
 Any decision to stay private or list its shares on stock exchanges, or even its choice of instruments for raising capital, lies exclusively with its shareholders; no third party can or should take that decision on their behalf. Any attempt to do so violates the natural order of a market-oriented economy. 
 RBI’s implicit logic that listing would engender transparency, leading to tighter regulation and better governance, does not stand scrutiny under standard risk metrics or the test of real-world examples; many listed companies in India have gone bust due to poor governance or lax regulatory oversight. 
 To be sure, a too-big-to-fail argument can be made for upper-layer NBFCs to be more transparent, but listing is not the only solution to that. 
 This is not to downplay RBI’s role in maintaining financial stability in the economy, which has several conglomerates as significant actors. 
 If RBI senses that there is even a sliver of risk in Tata Sons and its holding structure, the regulator can always spell out necessary guardrails for it; perhaps it can even nominate a director to the Tata Sons board for a closer line of sight into its operations, though this might need some enabling regulatory directives. 
 Additionally, if the central bank senses mounting risks, it can act in two ways. Directly, it can tighten regulatory compliance norms for the entity; indirectly, it can even exercise risk mitigation through the financial sector, like it did for virtual digital assets. But forcing a company to go public remains an unconvincing solution for risk avoidance. 
 In a recent public address, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said financial stability required proactive regulation “while being proportionate.” Pushing an entity, however large, to go public flies in the face of such a fair stance that balances systemic risks and the rights of shareholders. 
 Indeed, RBI’s energies may be better expended on a variety of risks that already dog the country’s financial services sector: digital fraud, cybersecurity threats as AI evolves, lending exuberance among NBFCs, a growing overhang of unsecured retail credit and climate transition shocks, among others.

News 
 BSNL pay scale freeze: why employees are threatening a strike
 Jatin Grover 5 min read 5 Oct 2026, 10:53 AM IST 
 Summary
 Employees want the government to relax the affordability rule for salary revision, while BSNL’s losses keep the proposal on hold 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A nine-year-old pay dispute between employees of state-owned Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd (BSNL) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) is escalating, with unions threatening a nationwide strike demanding implementation of salary revision.
 The All Unions and Association of BSNL (AUAB), a consortium of 15 employee unions of BSNL, has threatened a month-long agitation culminating in a nationwide strike on 20 November, according to a letter dated 18 September to the telecom secretary, Amit Agrawal.
 The unions are seeking implementation of the Third Pay Revision Committee (PRC) recommendations for BSNL executives and non-executives. The revision, which took effect for central public sector undertakings ( PSUs ) from 1 January 2017, has not been implemented at BSNL because the company does not meet the affordability criterion prescribed by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE).
 The clause requires PSUs to meet specified financial conditions, including profitability, before implementing a pay revision.
 “Since BSNL has been reporting losses, the company does not qualify under the existing norms,” a government official said. Any relaxation of the affordability condition would require Union cabinet approval, the official said, adding that the proposal is being examined by DoT, taking into account its financial and other costs.
 The unions are seeking a relaxation of the affordability condition, arguing that BSNL’s financial problems stem substantially from government policy decisions and management issues rather than employee performance.
 They said workers should not be penalised for the company’s losses and wanted BSNL to focus on profitable operations and avoid taking up loss-making projects.
 “BSNL is not working for profits as required under the affordability clause for implementation of third PRC and is working for implementation of all projects of government of India without looking into loss or profit,” said M.S. Adasul, general secretary of Sanchar Nigam Executives Association (SNEA), an employee association of BSNL.
 Adasul made these comments during a hunger strike and lunch-hour demonstration, part of the agitation programme, on 1 October at Eastern Court in New Delhi, adjacent to BSNL headquarters. The protest was part of the nationwide agitation programme. About 50 employees attended the demonstration in Delhi.
 “The non-implementation of pay revision over these years has already had an adverse impact on the family of many,” he said, adding that employees on deputation from DoT to BSNL are already enjoying the revised pay grade.
 Cost burden
 BSNL had 54,875 employees as of March-end, down sharply from 183,522 employees in March 2018. The reduction in workforce can be largely attributed to the voluntary retirement scheme (VRS) in 2019 and employee transfers.
 Employee costs fell to ₹ 7,439 crore in FY26 from ₹ 14,837 crore in FY18. As a share of revenue from operations, the cost declined to 35.6% from 65% over the same period. Revenue from operations stood at ₹ 20,919 crore in FY26, compared with ₹ 22,668 crore in FY18.
 BSNL's full-year loss was at ₹ 4,903 crore in FY26, compared with a ₹ 1,616 crore loss reported a year earlier.
 Its board had in 2017 submitted a proposal for pay scale revision of BSNL employees, recommending 15% fitment. As per BSNL's estimates then, the additional financial outgo on pay revision per annum for executives and non-executives with 15% fitment was ₹ 4,303 crore, according to a September 2025 note by All India BSNL Retired Executives’ Association.
 Fitment refers to the percentage benefit used to determine an employee’s revised basic pay under a new pay scale. The four options are 0%, 5%, 10% and 15%, with the highest option providing the largest increase in basic pay.
 The board sent a fresh proposal to DoT in February, according to employee union executives.
 Employee associations are also demanding arrears of their revised pay from 1 January 2017, when the pay revision was due to take effect. “We do not want to remain tied down to the old pay scale, which will create serious problems in the future,” P. Abhimanyu, vice-president of BSNL Employee Union, told Mint .
 “Look at the condition the government imposed on us, you cannot purchase equipment from foreign companies, you must buy from an Indian vendor…At least we should have been permitted to procure equipment from Nokia or at par with the private companies,” Abhimanyu said, adding that the quality of 4G equipment by domestic vendors is not up to the mark.
 Queries emailed to DoT and BSNL on Thursday remained unanswered.
 In a 10 March letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the All India Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited Executives’ Association said BSNL operates in an exceptional and highly dynamic environment” where telecom technology changes rapidly.
 “Employee compensation should be viewed as an investment in the revival of BSNL rather than merely a cost component,” the association had said, adding the company does not possess independent financial resources for acquiring advanced technologies without government approval.
 Despite these challenges, BSNL has achieved positive Ebitda in the last three financial years.
 However, due to other non-cash financial components, including depreciation, and finance cost, the company reported losses, it said.
 In FY26, the company’s depreciation and amortisation expense rose 64% year-on-year to ₹ 10,372 crore owing to higher capital expenditure.

docs.title: Jefferies initiates coverage on Dhoot Transmission: Here’s why it sees 14% upside
docs.text: Dhoot Transmission, a leading two-wheeler wiring harness manufacturer with a dominant position in electric vehicles (EV), is well positioned to benefit from rising demand as well as premiumisation due to stronger presence in faster-growing segments. The company is also expanding its component portfolio with battery packs, sensors, controllers, and power electronics. Global brokerage Jefferies has initiated coverage on Dhoot Transmission with a ‘Buy’ rating and has set a target price of Rs 1,730 apiece. This indicates a nearly 14% upside from the stock’s current level. “Its 43x 1-year forward PE appears rich but is justified, in our view, for its strong growth and franchise; our target is based on 42x September FY28 PE. Key risks to our estimates include weaker two-wheeler demand and slower electrification,” it said. The company derives 77% of its revenues from wiring harnesses and 23% from battery packs, sensors, controllers, and switches, as per Jefferies. Dhoot has a 41% market share in the two-wheeler and three-wheeler wiring harness in India. ALSO READRs 588 Bn exports, 90%+ rally: 2 stocks riding India’s aircraft-parts boom Jefferies on Dhoot Transmission: Earnings growth Jefferies expects the company to post a revenue growth of 24% on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) basis over FY26 to FY29. This translates into a 23% earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) growth on a CAGR basis over the same period and a 27% earnings per share growth. The company’s net cash is expected to rise to Rs 2,300 crore by FY29 from Rs 180 crore at the end of FY26. “While the cash build-up will dilute ROEs from 24% in FY26, we still expect healthy 16-18% over FY27-29E,” Jefferies said. Jefferies on Dhoot Transmission: Rising demand beneficiary The two-wheeler industry’s wholesale growth improved to 18-20% in FY27 and the second half of FY26 from 1% in the first half of FY26. Jefferies expects two-wheeler production in the country to rise 10% on a CAGR basis over FY26-FY29. “Two-wheeler demand has been shifting from small motorcycles to scooters and bigger bikes. Dhoot is well positioned to benefit from rising 2W demand as well as premiumisation given its higher content-per-vehicle and stronger presence in faster-growing segments,” the brokerage said. Jefferies on Dhoot Transmission: EV and broad portfolio The company has also established a strong presence in the EV wiring harness with 70% market share in both two- and three-wheeler EVs. “With 24% of FY26 revenues coming from EVs, Dhoot has one of the highest exposure to EVs within the listed auto-component space in India,” the brokerage said. “Dhoot is expanding its component portfolio with battery packs, sensors, controllers and power electronics. The recent acquisition of Multilink also broadens the product portfolio and adds HMCL as a customer, creating cross-selling opportunities. The company is pursuing a joint venture (JV) with Ride Vision for two-wheeler ADAS solutions and evaluating a high-voltage passenger vehicle harness JV,” Jefferies said. The company’s revenue, EBITDA and EPS are expected to grow in double-digits over FY26-FY29.

docs.title: HDFC Bank Q2 loans up 15%: Emkay sees 70% upside as Anup Bagchi takes charge
docs.text: It has been an eventful weekend for HDFC Bank. A new CEO was appointed bringing an end to weeks of uncertainty and the Q2 business update is out too. The private sector lender has remained in focus in recent months amid developments around its top management and business performance. Now, its latest business update has brought loan and deposit growth back into focus. According to the brokerage report by Emkay Global Financial Services, the brokerage has retained its 'Buy' rating on HDFC Bank with a target price of Rs 1,225. This translates into an upside potential of around 70% from the current market price. Let's take a look at the various developments that investors need to watch - HDFC Bank business update: The July to September report card HDFC Bank reported growth across both advances and deposits in the September 2026 quarter. Its average advances under management rose 14% year-on-year to Rs 3,18,720 crore from Rs 2,79,460 crore in the year-ago period. ALSO READ3 Largecap Stocks to Watch for the Long Term Investing Period-end advances under management stood at around Rs 3,30,750 crore, up 15.3% from Rs 2,86,880 crore a year earlier. Gross advances also increased 16.3% to around Rs 3,21,950 crore. Deposits recorded a faster pace of growth. Average deposits rose 16.8% year-on-year to Rs 3,16,650 crore. Within this, average current account savings account (CASA) deposits increased 10.7% to Rs 97,120 crore, while average time deposits rose 19.7% to Rs 2,19,520 crore. At the end of September 2026, total deposits stood at around Rs 3,32,750 crore, up 18.8% year-on-year. Furthermore, the period-end CASA deposits increased 10.8% to Rs 1,05,200 crore. Similarly, time deposits jumped 22.8% to Rs 2,27,550 crore. HDFC Bank Q2 update: How does this compare with Q1? The bank’s Q1 numbers provide another reference point for its business trajectory. Average advances under management stood at Rs 3,03,860 crore, while period-end advances under management were Rs 3,12,700 crore. Gross advances stood at Rs 3,06,100 crore. On the deposit side, average deposits stood at Rs 3,01,140 crore in June. Average CASA deposits were Rs 95,700 crore, while average time deposits stood at Rs 2,05,440 crore. Period-end deposits stood at Rs 3,17,050 crore, comprising Rs 1,02,550 crore of CASA deposits and Rs 2,14,500 crore of time deposits. Anup Bagchi’s appointment: Why is it important for HDFC Bank? On October 1, the Reserve Bank of India approved the appointment of Anup Bagchi, an ICICI Bank veteran and current Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of ICICI Prudential Life Insurance, as HDFC Bank’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer for a three-year period starting October 27, 2026. According to the Emkay report, “The approval is broadly in line with market expectations and media reports.” Emkay believes the appointment could help address uncertainty around the bank’s management transition. “We believe the appointment should help restore investor and customer confidence in the bank,” the brokerage said. Bagchi will also be the first chief executive from outside HDFC Bank’s organisation to lead the lender. According to Emkay, “His non-obtrusive leadership style, focus on broader strategic priorities, and aversion to micromanagement should help him carry the core team along.” ALSO READAnup Bagchi – strategist with an all-round experience is the new face of HDFC Bank HDFC Bank: What will the new management focus on? The brokerage expects management stability, deposit growth and branch productivity to remain key priorities. Technology and digital capabilities will also need attention, while processes will have to be strengthened to address issues seen in the past, including instances of mis-selling. “Overall, we believe this appointment should remove the prolonged overhang around management succession and help restore customer and investor confidence in the bank,” Emkay said. HDFC Bank: Why does Emkay see 70% upside? The brokerage believes HDFC Bank’s prolonged underperformance has brought its valuation to attractive levels. It expects progress in deposit and credit growth to support a potential re-rating. Emkay added that a sustained re-rating could depend on the bank delivering on its business priorities, while any moderation or reversal in foreign portfolio investor outflows amid easing geopolitical uncertainty could also influence the stock. docs.title: HDFC Bank to PNB: Motilal Oswal rates 6 banks ‘Buy’ as Q2 business updates roll in
docs.text: The banking sector is in focus as more than 23 banks announced their Q2 business updates over the weekend. Sustained retail demand, higher utilisation levels by MSME borrowers, healthy corporate borrowings, and higher-than-expected FCNR(B) flows are expected to support the growth momentum for domestic banks. Here is a detailed analysis of Motilal Oswal’s investment rationale - Motilal Oswal on HDFC Bank: Betting on new leadership HDFC Bank reported robust business growth for the second quarter of financial year 2027, in-line with expectations. Moreover, the bank’s appointment of Anup Bagchi as the new MD and CEO removes a “key overhang” around the leadership succession and brings external perspective at a time when the bank is trying to rebuild investor confidence, Motilal Oswal said. The stock is down 2.6% around Rs 702 intraday on Monday. “A new leadership team, alongside an improvement in growth and earnings trajectory, should improve investor sentiment,” Motilal said. It expects the bank’s earnings to improve from FY28 onwards. Motilal Oswal on Punjab National Bank: Global biz up 11% The brokerage has a ‘Buy’ rating on the public sector bank. PNB’s global business rose 11.95% on year to Rs 31.2 trillion in Q2 and domestic business was up 10.8% on year at Rs 29.7 lakh crores. Global advances increased 14.8% to Rs 13.4 lakh crore, led by lower growth in domestic advances. Motilal Oswal on Indian Bank: Steady business growth Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on Indian Bank. The bank’s total business grew 14.2% to Rs 15.96 lakh crore in Q2, with gross advances rising 16.6% to Rs 7.23 lakh crore. This growth was mostly driven by healthy traction in the RAM segment. Indian Bank’s deposits for the quarter rose 12.4% to Rs 8.7 lakh crore. Its CASA ratio was at 39.28% in the second quarter, slightly lower than 39.73% in the previous quarter. Motilal Oswal on Canara Bank: Growth traction across segments Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on Canara Bank. The bank’s total business grew 15.8% to Rs 30.7 lakh crore in Q2. Its global advances rose by 19.3% to Rs 13.7 lakh crore, led by good traction in the RAM segment. Canara Bank delivered healthy overall business growth, as per Motilal Oswal. Its global deposits were up 13.1% on year to Rs 16.9 lakh crore and domestic deposits grew 11% to Rs 15.5 trillion. ALSO READHDFC Bank Q2 loans up 15%: Emkay sees 70% upside as Anup Bagchi takes charge Motilal Oswal on AU Small Finance Bank: Loan portfolio in focus Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on AU Small Finance. The bank reported a nearly 28% on-year growth in gross advances to Rs 1.50 lakh crore. Its total loan portfolio rose 25.1% on year including the securitised and IBPC loan portfolio. Its CASA deposit growth was higher than overall deposit growth by 270 basis points sequentially at 10.8% to Rs 50,300 crore, resulting in CASA ratio improving to 29.5% from 28.8% as of Q1. “Overall business growth was healthy, with strong growth in CASA deposits. AU Bank remains our top pick in the mid-sized private bank space,” the brokerage said. Motilal Oswal on Equitas Small Finance Bank: Healthy advances Motilal Oswal has a ‘Buy’ rating on Equitas Small Finance. Its advances growth remains healthy, supported by strong mobilisation. The gross advances grew 29.6% on year and 6.4% sequentially to Rs 50,700 crore. Motilal Oswal on banking sector Motilal Oswal has rated the banks ‘Buy’ on a host of factors including healthy advance growth, steady ramp up of business and advances seeing a consistent upward trajectory. All eyes are now on the Q2 earnings of the banks.

docs.title: Rs 588 Bn exports, 90%+ rally: 2 stocks riding India’s aircraft-parts boom
docs.text: India’s aircraft-component manufacturing opportunity is expanding rapidly even before the country begins producing complete commercial aircraft at scale. A Frost & Sullivan analysis estimates India’s commercial-aircraft manufacturing market at ₹164.21 billion in 2026, up from ₹130.51 billion in 2024. It is projected to reach ₹257.09 billion by 2030, implying an 11.96% Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) during 2024–2030. The export opportunity is even larger. Ministry of Commerce data cited in an industry report shows India’s exports of aircraft and space parts jumped to ₹588.38 billion in FY25, from ₹269.03 billion in FY24 and ₹119.37 billion in FY19. This indicates a fast expansion of India’s participation in global aerospace supply chains. India’s expanding airline fleet backs demand. As of June 30, 2025, major Indian airlines had orders for 2,026 aircraft, according to data supplied by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to Parliament. Of these, 385 aircraft had already been imported by that date, leaving a substantial pipeline of aircraft to be inducted over the coming years. The scale of these orders is expected to support long-term demand across India's aerospace supply chain, including aerostructures, precision-machined components, electrical systems and assemblies. This creates a sizable opportunity for specialised suppliers serving global Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and Tier-1 aerospace companies, including Dynamatic Technologies and Aequs. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Dynamatic Technologies: From Detail Parts to Major Aerostructures Dynamatic Technologies operates across aerospace, hydraulics, metallurgy and security applications. Its aerospace business is conducted through Dynamatic-Oldland Aerospace and covers detail parts, sub-assemblies, assemblies and major assemblies. The company says its aerospace infrastructure delivers more than 800 aircraft shipsets annually and has manufactured more than 10,000 detail parts. Its customer base includes Airbus, Boeing, Bell Helicopter, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Dassault Aviation, Deutsche Aircraft and Prestwick Aerosystems, while its United Kingdom (UK) operations also serve Airbus UK, Boeing, GE Aviation, GKN Aerospace, Lockheed Martin, Spirit AeroSystems UK and AgustaWestland. Q1 FY27 Shows Operating Leverage, but Foreign Exchange (FX) Matters Dynamatic reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹424.81 crore in Q1 FY27, up 14.5% year-on-year (YoY) but down 1.9% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ). Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 45.9% YoY to ₹55.11 crore, taking the margin to 13%, while Profit After Tax (PAT) increased 92.9% YoY to ₹20.79 crore. The company said Q1 FY27 revenue would have grown 3.9% YoY on a constant-currency basis after removing a ₹39.26 crore favourable foreign-exchange impact. Constant-currency EBITDA would have been ₹49.97 crore instead of ₹55.11 crore. This means the underlying operating improvement was still positive, but headline growth overstated the underlying volume and execution momentum. Aerospace Is the Highest-Margin Business Aerospace revenue increased 17% YoY to ₹202.25 crore and represented 48% of Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue. Aerospace EBITDA rose 20.5% to ₹48.19 crore, while the EBITDA margin improved to 23.8% from 23.1% a year earlier and 20.7% in Q4 FY26. EBIT margin also increased to 17.8% from 16.8% in Q1 FY26. The company attributed the growth to execution across commercial aerospace and defence programmes and the ramp-up of detail-part programmes at Dynamatic Manufacturing Limited. The Airbus A220 doors programme also progressed during the quarter. The Rest of Dynamatic Still Matters Hydraulics generated ₹116.04 crore in Q1 FY27 revenue, up 9.4% YoY, while EBITDA rose 302.8% to ₹14.46 crore and the margin improved to 12.5% from 3.4%. Management attributed the improvement to product-mix optimisation and benefits from UK restructuring. Metallurgy generated ₹106.31 crore, up 15.7% YoY, with EBITDA rising 132.7% to ₹3.98 crore and the margin improving to 3.7%. This diversification changes how readers should view Dynamatic. It is not a pure-play aerospace stock. Aerospace provides the strongest margin profile and the largest revenue contribution, while the improvement in hydraulics and metallurgy is also supporting consolidated earnings. Consequently, future stock performance will depend on both aerospace execution and whether the non-aerospace businesses sustain their margin recovery. The wide swings in net profit show that revenue growth alone has not produced a stable earnings base, making the durability of the recent margin improvement more important than the pace of topline growth. Cash and cash equivalents were ₹54.12 crore, resulting in net debt of ₹473.14 crore. Including lease liabilities, overall debt stood at ₹577.42 crore. docs.title: 2.7X profit, 3X dividend growth, 3.7% yield: Is this PSU bank still undervalued?
docs.text: Welcome to the latest edition of Dividend Hunter. In recent weeks, we have analysed companies where strong cash flows could translate into consistent dividends. In our previous edition, we covered a public sector undertakingNBFC that delivered a 3.8% dividend yield. This week, in our 'Dividend Hunter' series, we are discussing a fast-growing and leading Indian public sector bank that has a market capitalisation of ₹1,19,365 crore as of October 1, 2026. In FY26, its total business crossed the ₹30 lakh crore milestone. Additionally, it recorded its highest-ever annual net profit of ₹20,021 crore. Notably, the bank's revenue grew at a 13% CAGR over the past five years, while net profit rose at a much faster CAGR of 72%. Alongside this, asset quality strengthened to a multi-year low, with Gross and Net NPA levels of 1.89% and 0.45%, respectively. The bank is also committed to sharing its financial success with shareholders. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now The bank maintains a clear policy to deliver periodic cash returns to its shareholders. For FY26, the Board recommended a dividend of ₹8.50 per share. In total, the bank paid a dividend of ₹4,395.7 crore during the year. It also boasts a Return on Equity of 15.39% and a Return on Assets consistently above 1%. Effectively, this public sector bank continues to balance capital appreciation with shareholder distributions. The bank is Bank of Baroda. Bank of Baroda Share Price Bank of Baroda Dividend Track Record: Why Profit Growth Outpaced Payouts Bank of Baroda paid a per-share dividend of ₹8.50 in FY26, translating into a dividend yield of 3.7% at the current price of ₹231.0. The bank issues a final dividend in June every year. Historically, the bank's per-share payout has almost surged 3x, from ₹2.85 in FY22 to ₹8.50 in FY26. In comparison, net profit grew by 2.75x during the period. Financial YearDividend/ShareNet ProfitPayout RatioFY22₹2.85₹7,272.0 crore19.0%FY23₹5.50₹14,110.0 crore19.0%FY24₹7.60₹17,784.0 crore22.1%FY25₹8.35₹19,581.0 crore22.0%FY26₹8.50₹20,021.0 crore22.0%Source: Annual Report The bank resumed dividend payments in FY22 after a four-year hiatus, following a period marked by high NPAs, elevated credit costs and losses. These challenges were common across the public sector banking space. The bank has also increased its payout ratio over the past five years, although at a slightly slower pace than its profitability. Core Operations: NII Inches Up 2.5% as Margin Contracts 19 bps to 2.89% Sustained financial growth enables Bank of Baroda to pay dividends. The bank's total business surged 13.9% year-on-year to ₹30,78,366 crore as global deposits grew 12.0% and advances surged 16.2%. Higher advances than deposits pushed the full-year Credit-Deposit ratio to a high of 91.65% against 88.56% in FY25 and 86.34% in FY24. The domestic Current Account Savings Account (CASA) ratio stood at 38.9%. Driven by strong business growth, the bank's total interest income grew 3.8% year-on-year to ₹126,994 crore. Of this, net interest income expanded 2.5% to ₹47,682 crore in FY26. Net Interest Margin (NIM), however, shrank by 19 bps to 2.89%. Source: Q4FY26 Investor Presentation The bank’s Cost-to-Income ratio also surged 121 bps to 49.15%, showing higher expenses. As a result, net profit grew only 2.2% to ₹20,021 crore. The Reserve Bank of India guidelines require dividends to be paid out of current-year net profits. In addition to net profits, dividend payouts depend directly on asset quality, capital adequacy metrics and regulatory guidelines. ALSO READAfter a decade without dividends, this PSU bank is back with a 3.8% yield Asset Quality Guardrails: Low NPAs Anchor Sustainable Cash Flows As of FY26, Retail, Agriculture, and MSME (RAM) financing accounts for 61.0% of gross domestic credit of ₹10,21,112 crore, while Corporate loans make up the remaining 39.0%. This mix has improved from FY25, when RAM advances held a 59.8% share. Balance Sheet Health: Why PCR at 93.9% Insulates Future Earnings About 96% of domestic advances above ₹50 crore carry external ratings of 'A and above’, which reduces default risk and stabilises asset performance. The bank's gross non-performing assets (NPAs) stood at a multi-year low of 1.89% (down from 2.26% as of Q4FY25), with net NPAs improving to 0.45% (down from 0.58%) in FY26. The bank’s Net NPA is well below the regulatory mandate of less than 7% required for dividend payout. The slippage ratio also fell by 6 bps to 0.72%, implying improved asset quality and fewer additions to stressed loans. A high provision coverage ratio (PCR) of 93.94% and ₹2,500 crore in floating provisions built up provide a strong buffer against any asset impairment losses. Overall, credit cost fell 1 bps to 0.46%. Keeping credit default risk low while maintaining strong capital buffers is key to sustaining asset quality, profitability and the bank’s capacity to distribute dividends. Deposit Profile: How a 38.9% CASA Base Shields Funding Costs At the same time, domestic deposits grew 12.8% year-on-year to ₹14,01,290 crore in FY26 (up from ₹12,42,169 crore in FY25), with domestic CASA at 38.9. This low-cost deposit base lowers the bank's funding costs, protects margins and also drives dividend payout. Capital Adequacy: 15.8% CRAR Provides Safe Headroom Over Basel III Norms Bank of Baroda's balance sheet maintains capital cushions comfortably above regulatory requirements, allowing consistent capital distribution to shareholders without restricting loan book expansion. In FY26, the Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) stood at 15.82%. CRAR further strengthened to 16.30% in Q1 FY27. The CRAR is significantly above the RBI-mandated threshold of 11.50% (including the mandatory 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer). docs.title: Bajaj Finance shares surge 4% as AUM growth hits 7-quarter high; brokerages positive
docs.text: Bajaj Finance shares rose 4.28% to Rs 988.85 in morning trade on October 5, as the company's September-quarter business update showed a strong acceleration in assets under management growth. AUM growth reached about 26% year-on-year, its highest pace in seven quarters, giving fresh support to the company's loan-growth story. Both Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Jefferies remain positive on Bajaj Finance. Motilal Oswal continues to count the company among its preferred non-bank finance names, while Jefferies has retained its ‘Buy’ rating. The two brokerages point to healthy loan growth and earnings momentum, although new loan bookings grew at a slower pace than a year earlier. Bajaj Finance AUM growth picks up as customer base expands Bajaj Finance's assets under management stood at Rs 5.85 lakh crore at the end of September, up 26.5% year-on-year and 6.9% sequentially, according to Motilal Oswal. The growth was ahead of the brokerage's estimate. The company booked 13.45 million new loans during the quarter, while its customer franchise continued to expand. New customer additions grew 7% year-on-year and the deposit book stood at Rs 69,800 crore. Jefferies also pointed to the stronger AUM performance. Prakhar Sharma and Vinayak Agarwal, equity analysts at Jefferies, said: “Bajaj Finance's pre-quarter release for September quarter shows an uptick in AUM growth to 26% YoY vs. 24% in June quarter, highest in 7 qtrs. Bajaj Housing Finance's AUM grew by 25%, implying the rest grew by 27% YoY. Growth in new loans booked (nos) slowed from 20% to 11% YoY, partly due to early festive season in the base when it had grown by 26% YoY.” ALSO READTCS, Infosys to Wipro: Jefferies sees earnings risk while Nuvama eyes upside for IT stocks Jefferies said Bajaj Finance added 4.4 million new customers during the quarter, taking its customer franchise to 129 million. The franchise grew 16% year-on-year and 4% sequentially. Bajaj Finance share price performance Motilal Oswal expects healthy September-quarter earnings Motilal Oswal expects Bajaj Finance to report a strong September quarter, with net interest income estimated to rise 22.5% year-on-year and 5.1% sequentially to Rs 13,210 crore. Operating profit is estimated at Rs 10,643 crore, up 19.9% year-on-year, while net profit is expected at Rs 6,372 crore, representing 28.8% year-on-year growth and 4.8% sequential growth. docs.title: Starting early, staying shallow
docs.text:
Sign In 
 CLOSE 
 For uninterrupted reading, switch to App
 READ IN APP 
 Written by Samiran Chakraborty 
 Updated: October 5, 2026 08:44 IST 
 Follow Us 
 The macroeconomic landscape has shifted considerably since the RBI’s August Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. Both globally and domestically, growth has demonstrated commendable resilience — but that is only half the story. Persistent geopolitical tensions have tilted inflationary risks sharply to the upside, prompting central banks worldwide to recalibrate their actions and guidance. Across developed and emerging markets alike, bond yields are rising, even as policymakers and market participants debate the underlying drivers of this dislocation and how long financial systems can absorb the pressure from elevated rates.
Against this altered backdrop, we expect the RBI MPC to reverse the rate cycle at its October meeting. The question of whether rates will rise has largely been settled — the more nuanced debate now centres on the quantum of the hike, the stance, revised forecasts and forward guidance, liquidity management measures, and any signals around the RBI’s currency view. Before examining these finer points, it is worth recapping the case for a rate hike in October.
Even at the August MPC meeting, the RBI’s own projections pointed to headline inflation in the 5.5-6.0% range over the following three quarters. With policy rates left unchanged, this implies uncomfortably low real rates and risks the perception of the central bank falling behind the curve — particularly given the direction of travel among global central banks and the trajectory of sovereign yields. Meanwhile, with GDP growth printing at a robust 7.8% year-on-year in Q1FY27, the RBI has little reason to fear a significant growth sacrifice from a moderate tightening move. If the central bank was holding out for greater confidence in its inflation outlook, developments over the past two months have provided clarity — though not of the reassuring kind. Every material data point signals upside, not downside, risk to the consumer price index (CPI) trajectory.
It is now highly likely that the October MPC will see meaningful upward revisions to both FY27 growth and inflation forecasts. On growth, we see 30-50 basis points (bps) of upside risk to the RBI’s FY27 real GDP forecast of 6.7%, given that Q1FY27 alone came in 80 bps above the central bank’s own estimate of 7.0%. On inflation, September CPI is tracking around 5.6% year-on-year, implying Q2FY27 inflation at approximately 5.0% — already 30 bps ahead of the RBI’s forecast. But the risks extend well beyond the September print. 
The diffusion index in August CPI climbed to its highest level since the series began in 2015, raising the spectre of generalised inflation likely to weigh on the MPC’s deliberations. Global crude oil prices remain near $100 per barrel, and petrochemical product prices have rebounded to March-April levels, with consequences for input costs and consumer prices alike. Wholesale price index manufacturing inflation, running above 8%, could eventually filter through to still-subdued CPI core goods inflation. 
A deficient monsoon is pressuring kharif crop prices, and with a strong El Niño expected to persist into early next year, risks to the winter crop are equally concerning. The World Bank’s EM Food Price Index has swung from -0.3% year-on-year in February to 11.5% in August — a reversal that cannot be ignored. Taken together, we see approximately 20 bps of upside risk to the RBI’s core inflation forecast of 4.3% for FY27, and around 10 bps to the headline forecast of 5.0%. The semi-annual Monetary Policy Report, due alongside the October decision, will provide the RBI’s first quarterly inflation estimates for FY28 — a critical input for markets gauging ex-ante real rates and the policy path into 2027 — and may also include a reassessment of the neutral rate.
The current MPC has consistently used the policy stance as a forward guidance tool, signalling the direction and duration of the rate cycle rather than committing to a terminal rate. October may be premature for the committee to declare a definitive endpoint. A neutral stance preserves flexibility and allows the MPC to frame a potential hike as a recalibration rather than the opening salvo of a prolonged tightening cycle. December, with the benefit of additional data, would be a more appropriate moment for a stance reassessment. Even so, the parameters the RBI flags as conditions for future hikes will be closely watched.
On liquidity, our projections suggest the current exceptional durable surplus will organically moderate by Q4FY27. It would therefore be prudent to allow overnight rates to adjust gradually toward the repo rate, rather than forcing an immediate convergence through aggressive withdrawal. Short-tenor sell/buy FX swaps and other FX interventions are likely to remain the primary absorption tools, offering maximum flexibility — though their effectiveness will be tempered by the limited depth of these markets. Additional open market operations sales of approximately `1.0 trillion are also possible, with an announcement potentially accompanying the policy statement.
If the MPC opts for a front-loaded 50-bps hike — premised on a baseline of 100 bps of cumulative tightening — it would carry hawkish overtones for markets, and would likely need to be accompanied by a stance shift to “calibrated tightening” and more assertive liquidity absorption. While such a package could bolster the RBI’s inflation-fighting credibility and support the currency in an era of rising global yields, it may be too aggressive a step so early in the cycle. Historically, the RBI tightening phases tend to be shallower and less protracted than those of its global counterparts, often reversing previous rate cuts without doing so in their entirety.
